html:
The Topasses, or Black Portuguese, were a mixed people of Portuguese, Timorese and other Asian descent who ruled much of western and central Timor in the 17th and 18th centuries. They spoke Portuguese and were Catholic.

From their base at Lifau in Oecusse, they controlled the sandalwood trade and fought both the Dutch and, at times, the Portuguese governors sent to rule them. Their leading families, such as the da Costa and Hornay clans, acted as kings.

In 1769 Topasses forced the Portuguese governor out of Lifau, and he moved the capital east to Dili. Their legacy is the Catholic, Portuguese-speaking identity of East Timor and of its enclave of Oecusse.
